definition: Needing a lot of hard, tiring effort, often over a long time.
example: Restoring the old farmhouse was an arduous project that took three summers.
nuance: Arduous stresses long, wearing effort; strenuous stresses intense physical exertion, and ardent (passionate) is only a look-alike.
prompt: A group of hikers spends several days climbing a steep mountain trail.
options: After four days on the arduous trail, the hikers finally reached the summit.
The hikers were arduous fans of the mountain and talked about it constantly.
The arduous trail was so gentle that even toddlers finished it in minutes.
From the ridge, the hikers admired the arduous colors of the sunset.
reasons: A steep, multiday climb takes sustained, exhausting effort, so the word fits.
This confuses the word with ardent; being enthusiastic is not the same as being difficult.
A gentle path that small children finish quickly is the opposite of hard and tiring.
Colors in the sky demand no effort from anyone, so the word has nothing to describe.

practice.prompt: A museum volunteer spends months cataloging thousands of handwritten letters.
options: The arduous task took her only a quick glance before her lunch break.
The arduous letters were written by sailors more than two centuries ago.
Sorting the faded letters by date was arduous work that filled most of her winter.
She was an arduous admirer of the letter writers and spoke of them with great warmth.
reasons: A job finished with a quick glance is easy, which reverses the meaning.
Being old does not make something hard to do; this mistakes the word for ancient.
Months of slow, careful sorting is the kind of draining labor the word describes.
Warm devotion calls for ardent; the word here should describe a task, not a feeling.
